title: Spatial conservation planning influences coral adaptive potential
content:
When selecting reefs for MPAs or other local interventions, the relative characteristics of reefs within the broader reef network influence marine conservation outcomes in a warming ocean. Hotter reefs are likely to contribute to network-wide resilience while receiving minimal in-network benefits. Colder reefs are likely to receive network benefits but can undermine network-wide resilience. Without these considerations, managers risk designing an MPA network that undermines its own resilience through negative spillover effects. Protecting diverse reefs in terms of connectivity and temperature may maintain adaptive capacity while avoiding negative eco-evolutionary feedbacks.


Abstract

The adaptive capacity of reefs to survive ocean warming and local stressors is driven by ecological and evolutionary processes occurring at multiple spatial scales. Marine protected area (MPA) networks, as regionally connected local interventions, may address both local and regional threats, yet the impacts of MPA network design on adaptive processes remain unclear. We used an eco-evolutionary model to simulate hypothetical MPA network configurations in the Caribbean, Southwest Pacific and Coral Triangle under an intermediate-emissions scenario (RCP 4.5). All MPA configurations increased overall regional coral cover relative to a simulation without MPAs, though none prevented an initial period of decline. We found that protecting thermal refugia (i.e. cooler reefs) largely benefited corals inside the MPA network, but allowed or even exacerbated decline elsewhere through spillover of colder-adapted alleles. In contrast, protecting the hottest reefs largely benefited reefs outside the MPA network via spillover of warmer-adapted alleles, with lesser benefits to reefs within the MPA network. Lastly, protecting a diverse habitat portfolio led to intermediate benefits both inside and outside of the MPA network. We then quantified the thermal habitat and connectivity of existing MPA networks across each region. Reefs in current MPA networks in the Southwest Pacific and Coral Triangle are approximately 2°C cooler than reefs outside the MPA networks, while the Caribbean's MPA network is approximately 1°C warmer than reefs outside the network. These results imply that the Caribbean MPA network is poised to protect sources of warm-adapted larvae but not destinations, and the opposite is true of the Southwest Pacific and Coral Triangle. Synthesis and applications: When selecting reefs for MPAs or other local interventions, the relative characteristics of reefs within the broader reef network influence marine conservation outcomes in a warming ocean. Hotter reefs are likely to contribute to network-wide resilience while receiving minimal in-network benefits. Colder reefs are likely to receive network benefits but can undermine network-wide resilience. Without these considerations, managers risk designing an MPA network that undermines its own resilience through negative spillover effects. Protecting diverse reefs in terms of connectivity and temperature may maintain adaptive capacity while avoiding negative eco-evolutionary feedbacks. These benefits assume future emissions reductions in accordance with RCP 4.5; MPA networks complement, but cannot substitute for, emissions reductions.
